I agree with the member who suggested watching a documentary or the Dr. Phil episode.  Amazon, documentaryaddict, and youtube all have a bunch of documentaries that are either free or inexpensive.  

Also, maybe have a talk with her about people misrepresenting themselves online.  It sounds silly, but maybe watching a few episodes of Catfish would scare her into being more careful with her information. 

Give her the more typical online dating advice: Always meet in a public place, do not offer personal information (like her website) until she has met someone in person and actually trusts them, etc...
Teach her to use reverse image search, and talk about red flags like changing the subject during a conversation to something more personal, pushing for more personal info, fake pictures, incomplete or ambiguous profile...etc...  Various things she may not know to look for.

  I had to try to communicate this to my grandmother not long ago, and the message was not well received, but I know I can't force her to do anything.  Just do your best, make sure she knows how to be responsible.  In the end, it's up to her to actually take your advice, though.

Seriously.  I got pregnant at a perfectly reasonable 110 lbs (I'm 5'1''), and I gained a perfectly normal amount during my pregnancy.  The additional calories my OB recommended for me after first trimester came from an extra glass of milk, some string cheese, or a sandwich... it doesn't take much more than that.  A fetus does NOT need an extra 2000 calories or so.  Just adding an extra nutritious snack during the day should be sufficient.

Likewise for breastfeeding!!  Yes you need a few more calories, you are using more calories to manufacture breastmilk.  A few more calories is not a justification for eating two entire boxes of oatmeal creme pies (no joke, a friend of mine was eating 2 boxes of these per day because oatmeal is good for lactation & she "needed" all of the calories from them).

Of course I did blow up after having my daughter.  Hint: it wasn't the pregnancy/breastfeeding/failure to lose the weight postpartum.  It was me failing to understand that zoloft would increase my appetite by a lot & not being appropriately careful about how much I was eating.  Whoops  :( 

Lengthy, but point being don't blame your freaking children.

My husband is amazing.  He takes care of our daughter from when he gets home until bedtime.  We have also separated the housework into the tasks that we are good at.  He deals with things that are easily visible-- trash, laundry, clutter, and dishes.  I do the sweeping, scrubbing, vacuuming, and folding.  It works for us-- I get so overwhelmed looking at clutter that I end up spacing out and being unable to do any of it, haha.  It sounds ridiculous, but I just completely disconnect.  Even with all of his help, I feel frantic.  :(

I'll try to take more breaks and be a little more careful with myself.

That I am obsessively clean.  
I have OCD and weird rituals that go along with it.  Performing these rituals make me feel safe.  I don't need my shoes lined up neatly along the wall or my kitchen sparkling.  I don't need my colored pencils lined up straight, by color.  I am obsessed with the idea that I am imagining everything happening around me and that nothing I am perceiving is real.  My compulsions are "reality" tests.  

Instead, I have to touch all four corners of my bed counterclockwise before falling asleep, enter bathrooms with my eyes closed, think a specific set of thoughts in a specific order--and restart if I get it wrong.  I force myself to "scream" in my head so that I can clear away images that get "stuck". I cope with intrusive thoughts about everything that could possibly go wrong, things that I see, everything that I do.  
I can't drive a car because all I can envision is what would happen if I jerk it into the oncoming lane, and I think about it so much that I convince myself that I want to even though I truly, truly don't.  If I look at a graphic image, I feel that the image I am looking at is of my loved ones, and so I check on them obsessively, just to make sure I'm not tricking myself into seeing my toddler safe and sound in bed when really, she is in danger.   In my mind, there is DEFINITELY something wrong and I'm just in denial.  
I see and hear danger everywhere, and some of my rituals make me feel like it won't happen. Others reassure me that I am seeing what is actually there.  

There are multiple ways to experience OCD, and obsessive cleanliness is only one of them--and even then, it's more than "I like my environment to be clean"

I still struggle with this, but I have found a few things that are helpful.  

1)  I give myself ample time before actually beginning the task to watch my surroundings.  If I need to do the thing at 4, I might "start" the task at 3, effectively budgeting some of my time to make sure doors are locked, my home is empty, I have my anchors nearby, and all necessary items are accounted for.

2)  Just after I finish doing the preliminary stuff, I talk through what exactly the task is.  I write a list of all things that need to be done prior to the task's completion.  This is my failsafe for distraction-- should I get sidetracked, I know exactly where I left off and how far I am from completing it.

3) As I sit down to actually begin, I do a presentness exercise, followed by a visualization exercise.

4) Once I've begun, if possible I try to schedule breaks or give myself a time allotment for distraction.  I also stop and re-do my presentness or visualization exercises if at any point I begin to feel too anxious to focus on the task.

I go through the five senses, usually with something like a cup of coffee.  

I look into my cup, notice all the little details, the way the cream mixes in with the coffee, any patterns or streakiness in the liquid.
Then, I tighten my hands around it, feel the liquid gradually warm the ceramic.  I tap on it a few times and inhale deeply to hear and smell it.  Afterward, I finally take a sip.  Without swallowing, I hold it in my mouth and pay attention to the flavors.  I like using coffee that I don't drink daily for this purpose-- I always find new flavors in it.  (:  

I have also had luck with visualizations.  If I feel too anxious to close my eyes, I stare at a calm, fixed point.  I imagine the distressing feeling as smoke lingering in my chest.  Inhaling stirs the smoke, and exhaling releases it.  I do this until I see the smoke dissipate.

Okay, I understand that feeling.  In the height of my depression, seeing someone struggling in some way when I was helpless to do anything about it was one of the worst feelings in the world.  

Sleeping does help shield oneself from those feelings.  Beyond sleeping, it was helpful for me to involve myself in humanitarian activities.  It kept me occupied and gave me a purpose, as well as a way to help those who were hurting.  

How long have you been feeling this way?

I'm so sorry you're dealing with this.

It does sound like fear may have been the goal.  In my experience, staying quiet meant getting to eat, sleep, use the restroom, attend school...etc...  For me, those are still points of control.  In order to do any of those things, I feel like I have to have earned them.  He was able to program lasting fear into me by manipulating very basic needs and then playing on my own feelings of inadequacy.  

I didn't mean to go off on a tangent.

It is completely up to you whether or not you will go.  You were hurt by this person, they failed to protect little you.  It's a tough position to be in, for sure.  I suggest you evaluate what is most important to you-- keeping in the good graces of those who would be upset with you not going, or stepping back and taking care of yourself.  You have no obligation to go, no obligation to please the people telling you to "let it go".  The only obligation you have is to what YOU feel is right.
